places.summary: Haryana's only hill station: pine-topped Shivalik ridges and the twin Tikkar Tal lakes.
places.seoTitle: Morni Hills: Haryana's Hill Station, Tikkar Tal, Treks
places.seoDescription: Morni Hills, 45 km from Chandigarh at 3,600 ft: Haryana's only hill station, with the twin Tikkar Tal lakes, an old fort, treks and the Mountain Quail resort.

overview.text: Morni is Haryana's only hill station, set in the lower reaches of the Shivalik range in Panchkula district at about 3,600 feet, some 45 km from Chandigarh and around five hours from Delhi. Pines crown the hilltops, and neem, oak, pipal, jamun, amaltas and jacaranda cover the slopes, so the hills turn bright with colour when the trees flower. The area is good for birdwatching, with quail, sand grouse and doves, and animals such as jackals, hyenas and sambar. Its best-known sight is Tikkar Tal, a pair of lakes separated by a hillock whose water levels always stay the same; locals consider them auspicious. A small temple on the bank holds a 12th-century Trimurti, and the ruins of an old fort recall Morni's past. Treks lead to the lakes, the fort and down to the Ghaggar river.

places.name: Pinjore Gardens (Yadavindra Gardens)
places.summary: A terraced 17th-century Mughal garden in the Shivalik foothills near Chandigarh.
places.seoDescription: Pinjore (Yadavindra) Gardens, 22 km from Chandigarh: a 17th-century terraced Mughal garden built by Aurangzeb's foster-brother and restored by the Patiala rulers.

overview.text: Pinjore Gardens, officially the Yadavindra Gardens, is a 17th-century Mughal garden in the town of Pinjore, Panchkula district, laid out in the Himalayan foothills. It was built early in Aurangzeb's reign by his foster-brother and architect Fidai Khan Koka, as a summer retreat, and was later renovated by the Sikh rulers of Patiala, whose Maharaja Yadavindra Singh gave it its present name. The garden is laid out in terraces with cypress avenues, fruit groves, fountains and the Jal Mahal pavilion, and an open-air theatre on the lowest level. It lies 22 km from Chandigarh, 87 km from Shimla and 255 km from Delhi, close to the 8th-century Bhima Devi temple complex, an open-air archaeological museum, and just 5 km from the UNESCO-listed Kalka–Shimla railway.

places.seoDescription: Karnal on the GT Road, 123 km from Delhi: the 'rice bowl of India', its walled old town and Karna Lake with boating and a Haryana Tourism resort.

overview.text: Karnal, on the Grand Trunk Road 123 km from Delhi and 130 km from Chandigarh, is one of Haryana's oldest districts and has been important since the Mahabharata era; it is often called the 'rice bowl of India'. The old city is a walled town, and its citadel, Kot Mohalla, was built by Raja Gajpat Singh of Jind; under the British it served as a residence for Dost Mohammad Khan of Kabul, a jail and a school. The astronaut Kalpana Chawla was born and went to school in Karnal, and Liaquat Ali Khan, Pakistan's first prime minister, was also born here. Today the city makes more than 40 percent of India's agricultural implements. For travellers its best-known stop is Karna Tank, named after King Karna, where you can go rowing or paddle boating beside Haryana Tourism's lakeside resort.

places.seoTitle: Narnaul: Jal Mahal, Birbal ka Chhatta, Ibrahim Khan Suri Tomb
places.seoDescription: Narnaul, Mahendragarh district: the Jal Mahal in Khan Sarovar, the five-storey Birbal ka Chhatta and the Lodi-style tomb of Sher Shah's grandfather.

overview.text: Narnaul, the headquarters of Mahendragarh district, is a small town with a surprising wealth of medieval buildings. Architecture from the Delhi Sultanate survives around the dargah of Shah Wilayat, and many Lodi-era buildings stand in the town and along the road to Delhi. Narnaul is likely the birthplace of Ibrahim Khan Suri, grandfather of Sher Shah Suri, who built him a monumental Lodi-style tomb here. The finest sight is the Jal Mahal, a pleasure palace in the middle of the Khan Sarovar tank, built under Akbar by Shah Quli Khan, governor of Narnaul for 52 years, and reached by a bridge on sixteen arches. Birbal ka Chhatta, a five-storey mansion of halls, pavilions and marble built by Rai Mukand Das, Diwan of Narnaul under Shah Jahan, takes its popular name from a legend that Akbar and Birbal visited.

places.seoDescription: Rewari Railway Heritage Museum, 50 km from Gurgaon: an 1893 steam loco shed with India's last steam engines and the 1855 Fairy Queen.

overview.text: The Rewari Railway Heritage Museum, 400 m north of Rewari station and about 50 km from Gurgaon, occupies the old Rewari Steam Locomotive Shed, built in 1893 on the line that once ran from Delhi towards Peshawar. For many years it was the only locomotive shed in north India. After steam on the metre gauge ended in January 1994 the shed lay neglected, until Indian Railways restored it as a heritage site; it reopened in 2002 and the refurbished museum opened in October 2010. It is now the only surviving steam locomotive shed in India and keeps some of the country's last steam engines, including the Fairy Queen of 1855, described as the world's oldest working steam locomotive. Alongside the engines are Victorian-era railway artefacts and old signalling equipment, and the locomotives are still fired up for live demonstrations.

places.name: Kalesar National Park
places.summary: Sal forests in the Shivalik foothills with leopards, elephants and jeep safaris.
places.seoTitle: Kalesar National Park: Safaris, Timings, Getting There
places.seoDescription: Kalesar National Park, Yamunanagar: Shivalik sal forest with leopards, elephants and birds; jeep safaris; closed July–September.

overview.text: Kalesar National Park lies in the Shivalik foothills of Yamunanagar district, 46 km from Yamunanagar city and 122 km from Chandigarh, next to the forests of Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand. Established in 2003, it adjoins the Kalesar Wildlife Sanctuary and is contiguous with Simbalbara National Park in Himachal and Rajaji National Park in Uttarakhand, forming a larger stretch of protected forest. The woods are mostly sal, with semul, amaltas and bahera, and the park is known for leopards, elephants and red junglefowl as well as excellent birdwatching. It takes its name from the Kalesar Mahadev temple inside the park, and a century-old colonial dak bungalow survives here. Wildlife jeep safaris run on three tracks. The park closes from July to September; in summer it is open 6–10 am and 4–7 pm, and in winter 7–11 am and 3.30–6 pm.
